documents.unit: Office of the Provost / Center for Teaching Innovation (CU Committee on Generative AI in Education)
documents.title: CU Committee Report: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Education and Pedagogy
documents.summary: A 2023 provost-convened committee report on generative AI in teaching. It recommends that each instructor adopt one of three postures (prohibit, allow with attribution, encourage), and gives guidance on integrity, privacy, equity, assessment, instructor use and administrative support.
documents.stance_why: The report sets no university-wide rule on student AI use: it proposes "a flexible framework in which instructors can choose to prohibit, to allow with attribution, or to encourage GAI use", so the decision is handed to instructors and the stance is delegates with three tiers.

units.why: The report proposes a framework where instructors choose among three postures, which is a rule about who decides and what the options are: "instructors can choose to prohibit, to allow with attribution, or to encourage GAI use". Chosen as P05 (named tiers) rather than P04 because it names the three categories; P04 is covered by the separate unit on faculty authority.
units.anchor: instructors can choose to prohibit, to allow with attribution, or to encourage GAI use

units.why: Opening framing: educators must account for GAI in learning objectives because "these technologies will not only be present in the future workplace, but are already being used by students". This is a principle for the institution, so a framework statement (P56) rather than a career rationale (P44), since it addresses educators' planning duty.
units.anchor: Educators must take generative artificial intelligence (GAI) into account when considering the learning objectives

units.why: The report names risks: "GAI tools can be used to circumvent learning" and hide "biases, inaccuracies, and ethical problems, including violations of privacy and intellectual property". This is a statement of harms, so P53 (bias, harms).
units.anchor: they may also hide biases, inaccuracies, and ethical problems, including violations of privacy and intellectual

units.why: The report charges the committee to recommend guidelines and ongoing evaluation: "Recommend guidelines for the safe and effective use ... Provide recommendations for ongoing evaluation and improvement". It states the purpose and scope of the institutional framework, so P56.
units.anchor: Recommend guidelines for the safe and effective use of AI technologies in an educational setting

units.why: Concern that lack of paid access "could exacerbate systemic inequalities" is an equity statement. P51 fits (access and cost) better than P53 because the concern is cost barriers.
units.anchor: lack of affordable access for all students could exacerbate systemic inequalities

units.why: The report warns that "overreliance on these tools risks atrophying students' ability and willingness to interact with instructors and peers". It is a harm of AI reliance on learning; P41 (AI shortcuts practice) is closest since P43 is about false mastery.
units.anchor: overreliance on these tools risks atrophying students’ ability and willingness to interact with instructors and

units.why: "We strongly encourage instructors to integrate GAI into learning outcomes" is a recommendation that instructors build AI into course goals, justified by students working in a "GAI-enabled world". P44 (teach AI as professional skill) fits; P02 is a student default rule, not this instructor-facing recommendation.
units.anchor: We strongly encourage instructors to integrate GAI into learning outcomes

units.why: "instructors must educate their students about the pitfalls of current technology. They must teach them to approach GAI critically and to validate GAI-produced information rigorously." Instructors are bound to teach critical verification; P31 (verify output) is the best home.
units.anchor: instructors must educate their students about the pitfalls of current technology

units.why: "They must teach them to approach GAI critically and to validate GAI-produced information rigorously" requires validation of AI output, so P31.
units.anchor: to validate GAI-produced information rigorously

units.why: "Instructors should clearly and consistently communicate to students their expectations on the use of GAI" asks instructors to state expectations in assignments and classes; P09 (state AI expectations) fits.
units.anchor: Instructors should clearly and consistently communicate to students their expectations on the use of GAI

units.why: "when GAI is permitted, it should be correctly attributed" sets a disclosure/attribution rule for students when AI is allowed, so P24.
units.anchor: when GAI is permitted, it should be correctly attributed

units.why: "Many foundational skills will still need to be developed without the use of GAI" and instructors "must directly explain to students why" shortcuts matter: a rationale that AI shortcuts practice, so P41.
units.anchor: instructors must directly explain to students why the process of achieving the specified learning outcomes

units.why: "To prohibit the use of GAI where it interferes with the student developing foundational understanding" names the prohibit option; it is one of the named tiers (P05), not a default.
units.anchor: prohibit the use of GAI where it interferes with the student developing foundational understanding

units.why: "To allow with attribution where GAI could be a useful resource" names the second tier, with the student taking "responsibility for accuracy and correct attribution". P05 for the tier definition.
units.anchor: allow with attribution where GAI could be a useful resource

units.why: "To encourage and actively integrate GAI into the learning process" names the third tier. P05 because it defines a named level.
units.anchor: encourage and actively integrate GAI into the learning process

units.why: Instructors can apply the three policies "either for individual assignments or generally in their courses", which leaves the decision per course or assignment: P04.
units.anchor: three kinds of policies either for individual assignments or generally in their courses

units.why: LLM output is described as plausible "regardless of the quality of the available evidence" and "New users often trust GAI models more than they should", which is a warning that output is unreliable; P31.
units.anchor: New users often trust GAI models more than they should

units.why: The report notes GAI "fluently create[s] plausible but false academic and other references", a fact about hallucinated citations, so P31.
units.anchor: GAI models also fluently create plausible but false academic and other references

units.why: Instructors should reassess outcomes: "instructors should reassess learning outcomes for each class in light of the advent of GAI". A course-design duty; P35 (redesign around AI) fits best.
units.anchor: instructors should reassess learning outcomes for each class in light of the advent of GAI

units.why: The calculator analogy states a staging principle: "prioritize students' learning basic skills without calculators at first, and later, allow and/or encourage their use". That is P08 (permission staged as skills develop).

units.why: Use of GAI "may appropriately be prohibited" when work "is meant to develop skills" such as practice problem sets or basic-skills assessment. A prohibition by situation; P41 (shortcuts practice) because the reason is skill-building.
units.anchor: the use of GAI tools may appropriately be prohibited

units.why: Students using tools "without properly citing them" is a concern, so "students [need] to learn to appropriately attribute and critique these tools". P24 attribution rule.
units.anchor: students use these tools without properly citing them

units.why: GAI use "should be encouraged" to promote accessibility or enhance high-level learning and creativity. A permission/encouragement rule: P02.
units.anchor: the use of GAI should be encouraged

units.why: Free access makes it tempting to "turn in AI-generated content as their own", a statement of misuse concern. P19 closest (don't submit AI work as own) as an informs-level rationale.
units.anchor: violate academic integrity principles by turning in AI-generated content as their own

units.why: Detectors like TurnItIn and GPTZero "cannot decisively provide evidence of academic integrity violations" and could cause unfair accusations. P39 (do not rely on detectors).
units.anchor: cannot decisively provide evidence of academic integrity violations

units.why: Detection could "unfairly identify[ing] academic integrity violations (for example, bias against non-native speakers)". Fairness harm of detectors, still P39 (not P53) because it concerns detector reliability.
units.anchor: Using these methods currently could lead to unfairly identifying academic integrity violations

units.why: Provider restrictions are described as not foolproof because of jailbreaks: "the barriers have not proven to be foolproof". It is a fact about technical enforcement limits; no type fits exactly, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: the barriers have not proven to be foolproof
units.uncovered_note: Technical restriction of AI outputs by providers or university-run restricted services is considered but judged not foolproof (jailbreaks).

units.anchor: if students rely on GAI, they will not put in the practice needed to learn

units.why: "Instructors should communicate to students why completing assignments without 'shortcuts' is necessary". Explaining the rationale to students; P41.
units.anchor: Instructors should communicate to students why completing assignments without “shortcuts” is necessary to meet learning

documents.title: AI & Academic Integrity
documents.summary: Center for Teaching Innovation guidance for instructors on communicating AI policy, with four sample syllabus statements, advice on handling suspected violations and evidence, citation of AI, and a recommendation against detectors.
documents.stance_why: The page offers sample statements ranging from "AI-FREE" to "ANY-AI-UA" and "AS" ("decided on an assignment-by-assignment basis") and does not itself set a rule, so it delegates with tiers.

units.why: "be sure to clearly communicate your policies regarding the use of generative AI in your syllabus, in assignment instructions, and verbally in class" directs instructors to state policy in three places. P09.
units.anchor: clearly communicate your policies regarding the use of generative AI in your syllabus, in assignment

units.why: "When generative AI is permitted, clarify expectations for documentation and attribution, as well as what aspects of the work should be produced by the students themselves." P24.
units.anchor: clarify expectations for documentation and attribution

units.why: "they are responsible for verifying the output and references if AI use is allowed". Student verification duty, P31.
units.anchor: they are responsible for verifying the output and references if AI use is allowed for

units.why: Course policy icons "help Cornell instructors communicate with students about appropriate AI use for different courses and assignments". Icons are tiers for communicating policy: P05.
units.anchor: to help Cornell instructors communicate with students about appropriate AI use for different courses and

units.why: "faculty should clearly define for students both your expectations and their responsibilities around using generative AI tools". P09.
units.anchor: faculty should clearly define for students both your expectations and their responsibilities

units.why: "Require that students verify the accuracy of all citations and references they include in their work." P31.
units.anchor: Require that students verify the accuracy of all citations and references they include

units.why: "Request that students provide verification of references or methods", with the response determining whether a formal notification is warranted. Process evidence of understanding; P34.
units.anchor: Request that students provide verification of references or methods

units.why: "Clearly limit allowable methods, tools, or references, and specify that deviations ... could constitute evidence of potential integrity violations." Treats unauthorized use as misconduct evidence: P36.
units.anchor: specify that deviations from these restrictions could constitute evidence of potential integrity violations

units.why: "Inform and remind students that they should expect to verbally explain the work they submitted." P30.
units.anchor: they should expect to verbally explain the work they submitted

units.why: The AI-FREE template says "the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools is prohibited" to ensure mastery of foundations. Course-wide ban: P01.
units.anchor: the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools is prohibited

units.why: AI-FREE sample extends the ban to "tools that help reorganize and edit your written work". Rule for prose tools, P18.
units.anchor: tools that help reorganize and edit your written work

units.why: "please consult with me prior to using the technology" if unsure, including whether a tool counts as generative AI. P10.
units.anchor: please consult with me prior to using the technology or completing your assignment

units.why: "You will be asked to verbally explain your research and writing process during in-class discussions and in a one-on-one meeting." Oral check of understanding: P34.
units.anchor: You will be asked to verbally explain your research and writing process

units.why: "You are responsible for verifying the accuracy of citations and references used in your writing." P31.
units.anchor: You are responsible for verifying the accuracy of citations and references

units.why: "appropriate and ethical use of generative AI tools will likely be a part of other courses in your academic program" tells students the ban is course-specific. P11.
units.anchor: appropriate and ethical use of generative AI tools will likely be a part of other

units.why: AS-UA template: AI "is generally discouraged in this course, but will be permitted for select assignments". Discourages without forbidding: P03.
units.anchor: the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools is generally discouraged in this course

units.why: "Whether or not generative AI assistance is permitted for each assignment will be explicitly communicated when that assignment is introduced." Assignment-level decision: P04.
units.anchor: Whether or not generative AI assistance is permitted for each assignment will be explicitly communicated

units.why: "generative AI requires proper attribution for any and all generated work". P24.
units.anchor: generative AI requires proper attribution for any and all generated work

units.why: Students "should attribute directly quoted text to the creator of the generative AI tool used (e.g., cite OpenAI when directly quoting ChatGPT)". Names the tool in the citation: P25.
units.anchor: students should attribute directly quoted text to the creator of the generative AI tool used

units.why: "it is critical that you adhere to our communicated course policy (and Cornell's policy) on academic integrity" whether or not AI is permitted. Ties AI to integrity rules: P36.
units.anchor: it is critical that you adhere to our communicated course policy

units.why: The ANY-AI-UA template says "The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools is encouraged on identified assignments." P02.
units.anchor: The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools is encouraged on identified assignments

units.why: "If used at all, generative AI requires proper attribution for any generated work." P24.
units.anchor: generative AI requires proper attribution for any generated work

units.anchor: Evidence of an academic integrity violation needs to meet a clear and convincing standard

units.why: "transparency is key, and these instances should be properly referenced" for LLM material in assignments. P24.
units.anchor: transparency is key, and these instances should be properly referenced

units.anchor: include an AI-generated source in the methods section of their research paper

units.why: "if instructors choose to use LLMs to help in the preparation of course materials, such work should be acknowledged and attributed." P48.
units.anchor: such work should be acknowledged and attributed

units.why: "it is unlikely that detection technologies will provide a workable solution" and tools "cannot provide evidence for that claim". P39.
units.anchor: it is unlikely that detection technologies will provide a workable solution

units.why: "This raises a substantial risk that students may be wrongly accused of improper use". Accuracy risk of detectors: P39.
units.anchor: students may be wrongly accused of improper use of generative AI

notes: Only the two included university-layer documents were coded. No school or computing-unit policy found; course layer deferred in collect file. The committee report was coded as written in 2023; the CTI page is current guidance. Two units are UNCOVERED (technical restriction by providers not foolproof; Canvas integrity-reflection module).
